safi-cedvel:1-1.t:
* I'rab:
(بسم) a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate). The mubtadaʾ (subject) is omitted, its implied form being "ابتدائي" (my beginning).
(الله) the Name of Majesty, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), and the sign of the genitive is the kasra. (الرحمن) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive. (الرحيم) a second naʿt of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive.

* Morphology:
(اسم) contains ibdāl (substitution); its origin is سمو. The weak letter, which is the lām (third radical) of the word, was deleted, and the hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was substituted for it. The proof of the wāw is its plurals أسماء and أسامي and its diminutive سمىّ. The originals were أسماو, أسامو and سموي, and iʿlāl (weak-letter change) by qalb (conversion) took place in them.
(الله) .. its origin is الإلاه: the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lām of the definite article, then it was made vowelless; the first alif was deleted because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and the lām was assimilated into the second lām..
The alif after the second lām was deleted because of frequent use. الإله is a maṣdar (verbal noun) from أله يأله, meaning "to worship", and the maṣdar stands in the place of the object, i.e. "the one worshipped".
(الرحمن) a derived adjective of the intensive forms; its pattern is فعلان, from the verb رحم يرحم, of the class of فرح.
(الرحيم) a derived adjective of the intensive forms, or an adjective resembling the active participle (ṣifa mushabbaha); its pattern is فعيل, from the verb رحم يرحم.

* Rhetoric:
1- Repetition (al-takrīr): Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated the mention of الرحمن الرحيم because mercy is the bestowal of favour on one in need. He had mentioned the Bestower without those on whom favour is bestowed, so He repeated it together with mentioning them and said: «ربّ العالمين الرحمن» to them all.
2- He, Glorified is He, put الرحمن before الرحيم although الرحمن is more intensive than الرحيم, while it is the custom of the Arabs in attributes of praise to ascend from the lower to the higher, as in their saying: "So-and-so is a learned man, a consummate scholar (عالم نحرير)". That is because it is a name exclusive to Allah the Exalted, like the word «الله», and because when He said «الرحمن» it covered the great and mighty favours and their roots, and He followed it with «الرحيم» as a completion and a sequel, to cover the fine and subtle among them. What belongs to the great and mighty favours and their roots is more deserving of being put first than what indicates their fine points and branches. And singling out these two noble attributes for mention is to set the chain of mercy in motion.
By the name of Allah the Exalted the meanings of things are completed, and from the lamp-niche of بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ the lights of splendour shine upon the pages of the universes.

* Benefits:
The Basmala:
The scholars took care to study the Basmala from all its aspects, of which we mention in particular:
1- They differed over whether it is a verse of the Book of Allah or not. Ibn Masʿūd, Mālik, the Ḥanafīs and the readers of Medina, Basra and Syria do not consider it a verse.
Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shāfiʿī and the readers of Mecca and Kufa consider it a verse of every surah.
2- The Basmala was revealed in parts: the first part in the saying of the Exalted: «بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْراها وَمُرْساها»; the second in His saying: «ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوِ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمنَ»; the third in His saying: «إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ».

safi-cedvel:2-2.t:
* I'rab:
(الحمد) mubtadaʾ (subject), nominative (marfūʿ). (لله) a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ, its implied form being ثابت (established) or واجب (due). (ربّ) naʿt (adjective) [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty.] of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra. (العالمين) muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), and the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ, because it is assimilated to the sound masculine plural.
The clause «الحمد لله..» has no grammatical position, being initial (ibtidāʾiyya).

* Morphology:
(الحمد) a heard (samāʿī) maṣdar (verbal noun) of the verb حمد يحمد, of the class of نصر; its pattern is فعل, with fatḥa then sukūn. (ربّ) a maṣdar of يرب, of the class of نصر, then used as an adjective, like عدل and خصم; its pattern is فعل, with fatḥa then sukūn.
(العالمين) plural of العالم, which is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) having no singular from its own letters. It is derived either from العلم (with kasra on the ʿayn) or from العلامة; its pattern is فاعل with fatḥa on the ʿayn, and likewise its plural.

* Rhetoric:
1- The clause الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ is a statement (khabar), but it is used to perform (inshāʾ) the praise, and the benefit of the nominal clause is the perpetuity, continuity and constancy of the praise. In His saying «لله» there is the device of specification (al-ikhtiṣāṣ), to indicate that all praises are exclusive to Him, Glorified and Exalted is He.
2- Since He, Glorified and Exalted is He, opened His Book with the Basmala, which is a kind of praise, it was fitting that He follow it with the comprehensive, universal praise encompassing all its individual instances and reaching the utmost degree of perfection.
3- As for Allah the Exalted praising Himself, it is a statement that He deserves praise and a command to it, or it is said on the tongues of the servants, or it is a figurative expression for the manifestation of the attributes of perfection, which is the ultimate goal of praise.
Praise has been put before the Majestic Name because the context calls for a singular concern with it, even though the mention of Allah the Exalted is more important in itself, and importance calls for putting first.

* Benefits:
Al-Fātiḥa:
Its benefits can hardly be counted; we choose from them:
1- The revelation brought it down twice: the first in Mecca when the prayer was made obligatory.
The second in Medina when the qibla was changed.
2- Al-Fātiḥa has several names: Fātiḥat al-Kitāb (the Opening of the Book), Umm al-Qurʾān (the Mother of the Qurʾān), Umm al-Kitāb (the Mother of the Book), Sūrat al-Kanz (the Surah of the Treasure), Sūrat al-Ḥamd (Praise), al-Shukr (Thanks) and al-Duʿāʾ (Supplication), Sūrat al-Ṣalāh (the Prayer), Sūrat al-Shifāʾ (Healing), and al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī (the Seven Oft-Repeated).
3- The style of iltifāt (shift of address) occurs in this surah: it began by speaking of the absent, then turned to the style of direct address, and this is one of the kinds of eloquence common in the speech of the Arabs.
4- Al-Fātiḥa contains the basic universals of the Islamic conception, and for that reason Allah made its repetition obligatory in every prayer, indeed in every rakʿa.
It has come in the hadith of Muslim from Abū Hurayra from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ his saying: «Allah the Exalted says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. When the servant says: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ, Allah says: My servant has praised Me. And when he says: الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ, Allah says: My servant has extolled Me.
When he says: مالِكِ يَوْمِ, Allah says: My servant has glorified Me. And when he says: اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ, He says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked».

safi-cedvel:3-3.t:
* I'rab:
(الرحمن) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty, and likewise الرحيم.]. (الرحيم) a second naʿt of the Name of Majesty.

safi-cedvel:4-4.t:
* I'rab:
(مالك) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty.], genitive (majrūr) like it. (يوم) muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra.
(الدين) muḍāf ilayhi, genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra.

* Morphology:
(مالك) active participle of ملك يملك, in the sense of the ṣifa mushabbaha (adjective resembling the participle) because of the permanence of the ownership; of the class of ضرب; its pattern is فاعل; its plurals are ملّاك and مالكون.
(يوم) a noun meaning the defined time from sunrise to sunset, or an undefined time. Here it comes in the sense of the Day of Resurrection. Its plural is أيّام, and the plural of the plural is أياويم.
(الدين) maṣdar (verbal noun) of دان يدين, of the class of ضرب, meaning "to requite" and "to obey" or "to submit"; its pattern is فعل, with kasra on the fāʾ and sukūn on the ʿayn. There is another maṣdar of the verb, namely ديانة with kasra on the dāl. الدين means requital or obedience, and it may mean religion (al-milla) or custom.

safi-cedvel:5-5.t:
* I'rab:
(إيّاك) an overt, detached pronoun, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, in the position of the accusative as a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object); or (إيّا) is an indeclinable pronoun in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl bihi, and (الكاف) is a particle of address. (نعبد) imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), and the fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, obligatorily so, its implied form being نحن (we). (الواو) is a conjunction. (إياك نستعين) is parsed like the preceding.
The clause «إياك نعبد..» has no grammatical position, being resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya).
The clause «إياك نستعين..» has no grammatical position, being conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to the clause إياك نعبد.

* Morphology:
(نستعين) contains iʿlāl (weak-letter change); its origin is نستعون, from العون, with kasra on the wāw. The kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was transferred to the ʿayn and the wāw was made vowelless — this is iʿlāl by taskīn (making vowelless) — then the wāw was converted to yāʾ because it is vowelless and preceded by a kasra — this is iʿlāl by qalb (conversion).

* Rhetoric:
1- Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated «إيّاك» because, had He omitted it in the second, the benefit of the fronting would have been lost, namely cutting off the sharing between the two governing verbs. For had He said: «إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ ونستعين», it would not have been clear whether the implied meaning is "إيّاك نعبد وإيّاك نستعين" or "إيّاك نعبد ونستعينك". And He did not say نستعينك, although it would serve to cut off the sharing between the two governing verbs, so that it would convey restriction (al-ḥaṣr) between the two governing verbs.
He put worship before seeking help, although seeking help comes first — because the servant seeks the help of Allah in worship so that He may help him in it — because the wāw does not require order, and seeking help is the fruit of worship, and because presenting the means before asking for the need is so that they may merit having it answered.
2- The iltifāt (shift) in this noble verse is a shift from the absent (third person) to the second person, a variation of the composition from one mode to another, running according to the way of eloquence in diversifying speech and the path of excellence as the context requires. For moving from one style to another is more effective in drawing souls and winning hearts; it occurs from each of the first person, the second person and the third person to each of the other two, as in the saying of the Exalted «اللَّهُ الَّذِي أَرْسَلَ الرِّياحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحاباً».
3- Preferring the form of the speaker together with others in the two verbs is to announce the speaker's own shortcoming and his unfitness to stand alone in the stations of grandeur, presenting worship and calling for help and guidance independently; and that this is conceivable only from a band of which he is one and a group of whose company he is part, as is the custom of kings. Or it is to indicate that all the monotheists share with him in the state that has come upon him, based on the mutual support of the proofs compelling that.

safi-cedvel:6-6.t:
* I'rab:
(اهد) imperative verb of supplication, indeclinable (mabnī) on the deletion of the weak letter, and (نا) is an attached pronoun, indeclinable, in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, obligatorily so, its implied form being أنت (you). (الصراط) second mafʿūl bihi, accusative (manṣūb), and the sign of the accusative is the fatḥa [Note: The verb (هدى) is transitive to the second object without a preposition, or with the preposition اللام, or with the preposition إلى. It is stated in al-Muḥīṭ: هداه الله الطريق, وله, وإليه.].
(المستقيم) naʿt (adjective) of الصراط, accusative like it, and the sign of the accusative is the fatḥa.
The clause has no grammatical position, being resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya).

* Morphology:
(اهدنا) contains iʿlāl (weak-letter change) by deletion, to suit the indeclinability; its origin in the nominative imperfect is تهدينا. The pattern of اهدنا is افعنا. (الصراط) is with sīn and with ṣād; in the reading with ṣād there is ibdāl (substitution), as the sīn was converted to ṣād to harmonise with the ṭāʾ in iṭbāq (velarisation).
(المستقيم) active participle of استقام; it is on the pattern of its imperfect, replacing the imperfect prefix with a mīm carrying ḍamma and putting kasra on the letter before the last.. It contains iʿlāl; its origin is مستقوم — with kasra on the wāw — because its bare verb is قام يقوم; then the same happened in it as happened in نستعين.

* Rhetoric:
1- «اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ»: المستقيم means the level (straight), and what is meant by it is the path of truth, namely the tolerant ḥanīf religion, midway between excess and negligence. The true religion is likened to the straight path, and the point of similarity between them is that Allah, Glorified is He, though exalted above places, yet the servant seeking to arrive must cross distances, so that the arrival and the meeting may be honoured. This is of the type of explicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-taṣrīḥiyya).
2- He, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated the mention of «الصراط» because it is the place prepared for travelling. In the first He mentioned the place without the traveller, so He repeated it with mention of him in His saying «صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ», in which it is made explicit what excludes the Jews, who are those who incurred wrath, and the Christians, who are those astray.

safi-cedvel:7-7.t:
* I'rab:
(صراط) badal (substitute) of the first صراط, following it in the accusative, and the sign of its accusative is the fatḥa. (الذين) relative noun, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, in the position of the genitive as muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). (أنعمت) past verb, indeclinable on the sukūn because it is attached to a nominative pronoun, and (التاء) is an attached pronoun in the position of the nominative as fāʿil (agent). (عليهم): (على) is a preposition and (الهاء) is an attached pronoun, indeclinable on the kasra, in the position of the genitive by (على), attached to (mutaʿalliq) (أنعمت); and (الميم) is a particle for the masculine plural. (غير) badal of the relative noun (الذين), following it in the genitive [Note: Or badal of the pronoun in (عليهم), or naʿt (adjective) of the relative noun. This last is rejected by al-Mubarrad, because (غير) for him can only be indefinite even if it is put in construct, the construct in it being merely verbal (lafẓiyya), while (الذين) is definite.. This objection has been answered with two answers:
The first: that (غير) is indefinite when it does not fall between two opposites; but when it does — as in the preceding verse — the otherness is confined, and so it becomes definite through the construct.
The second: that the relative noun resembles indefinite nouns in the vagueness it contains, so it was treated as indefinite nouns are treated.]. (المغضوب) muḍāf ilayhi, genitive. (عليهم) like the first, in the position of the nominative as nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of المغضوب. (الواو) a conjunction. (لا) redundant (zāʾida), to emphasise the negation. (الضالّين) maʿṭūf (conjoined) to (غير), genitive like it, and the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural.
The clause أنعمت عليهم ... has no grammatical position, being the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun.

* Morphology:
(المغضوب) passive participle of غضب, of the class of فرح; its pattern is مفعول.
(الضالّين) plural of الضال, which is the active participle of ضلّ يضلّ, of the class of ضرب; its pattern is فاعل, and the ʿayn of the word was assimilated into its lām because they are the same letter.
(غير) a noun that is always singular and masculine; it may be a naʿt (adjective) and it may be a particle of exception..
If a feminine is intended by it, it is permissible to make the verb attributed to it feminine. You say: قامت غير هند, meaning thereby a woman.. It is always in construct, overtly and implicitly. So putting the alif and lām on it is an error.

* Rhetoric:
1- Explanation after vagueness (al-tafsīr baʿd al-ibhām): in this noble verse, where it is made clear that the straight path — its exposition and explanation — is the path of the Muslims, so that this is a testimony to the path of the Muslims as being straight in the most eloquent manner; as you say: "Shall I direct you to the most generous and most excellent of people? So-and-so." This is more eloquent in describing him with generosity and excellence than your saying:
"Shall I direct you to So-and-so, the most generous, the most excellent?" because you have mentioned him twice, first in summary and second in detail, and you made So-and-so an explanation and clarification of "the most generous, the most excellent", and so you made him a byword for generosity and excellence.
2- Rhyming (al-tasjīʿ): in الرحيم and المستقيم, and in نستعين and الضالين. Tasjīʿ is the agreement of two words in pattern and in the rhyme letter (al-rawī).
3- And if we consider what is the benefit of the entry of «لا» in the saying of the Exalted «وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ», although the speech without it would suffice for the purpose: it is to emphasise the negation conveyed by «غير».
4- The opening (al-istihlāl):
Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, opened the Qurʾān with al-Fātiḥa, and istihlāl is one of the finest and most elegant devices of rhetoric. Its definition: that the speaker begins his speech with what points to the intended aim without being explicit, but by a subtle allusion.
5- Turning away from attributing anger to Him the Exalted, as was done with bestowing favour, follows the method of the courtesies of the revelation in attributing favours and good things to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, but not their opposites, as in the saying of the Exalted: الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ وَالَّذِي هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِي وَيَسْقِينِ وَإِذا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ
